newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends strong vs yen, at highs vs mark in US.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends strong vs yen, at highs vs mark in US.

text.p: The dollar rose sharply against the mark and posted solid gains versus the yen on Monday in a U.S. session characterized by broad mark weakness and ample yen strength on the crosses.
As the day unfolded, the greenback benefitted from dwindling dollar/yen sales as well as heavy purchases of yen and sterling for marks.
"Mark/yen and sterling/mark have certainly been the flavors of the day after the big yen move overnight," said Seth Garrett, chief dealer at Credit Suisse First Boston.
The dollar ended the day at 1.7070/80 marks, up from 1.6927/32 at the open. It rose to 119.30/40 yen against 118.55/60.

The dollar's rise during U.S. trading hours came after substantial losses in early Asian dealings, which took the greenback to a near-four month low of 117.50 yen and to its lowest level against the mark in more than a month.

The source of the early losses was remarks from key Japanese Ministry of Finance official Eisuke Sakakibara, who told reporters over the weekend that the dollar's sharp seven-yen slump last week had not been excessive.
Once the lows were hit, however, the dollar began a slow but steady climb, ultimately rising almost four pfennigs and roughly two yen by the U.S. close.

Damage control by Japanese officials, including Sakakibara himself, got the ball rolling. But dealers said that a shift from dollar/yen sales to active mark/yen selling during U.S. hours was the primary reason for the greenback's recovery.
"There continues to be good yen buying across the board," said Ben Strauss, assistant vice president at Bank Julius Baer.
"But it has shifted from buying against the dollar to the buying of yen against the European currencies, which has, in turn, aided the dollar against Europe," he added.
Mark/yen slumped to a near-one year low of 69.67 on Monday and sterling/mark gained, rising as high as 2.7718 after remarks from Britain's new Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown.

Brown said on Monday he had no plans to take the pound back into Europe's exchange rate mechanism. Reports last week that Britain was considering re-joining the ERM at a central rate of 2.50 marks had sent sterling lower versus the mark.
"People took back some of their short sterling positions on that," said John McCarthy, senior vice president at ING Barings Capital Markets.

Dealers said the dollar's ability to close above 1.7050 marks was impressive and predicted further gains in the days ahead. They were less optimistic about dollar/yen, however, calling for a new near-term range between 115 and 120 yen.
"We've definitely taken the edge off and made it a bit more of a careful decision to go in and buy dollar/yen," said McCarthy.
In other trade on Monday, the dollar ended at 1.4378/88 Swiss francs, up from 1.4272/82 at the open. It retreated to Canadian $1.3892/97 from C$1.3920/25.
The British pound rose to $1.6230/40 from $1.6165/70, while the Australian dollar settled at $0.7785/90, slightly lower than its opening rate of $0.7791/96.
